scenes.title: Frozen bread
scenes.narration: January, 1709. The wine is freezing in the barrels. The bread on my shelves is frozen so hard. I have to cut it with an axe. And outside my bakery, the whole town is waiting. My name is Étienne. I am a baker. And this is how my family survived the coldest winter in five hundred years.

scenes.narration: Everything in my life turns around one thing: the oven. A dome of brick and stone, as old as the house. Once it is hot, it holds the heat for hours. It feeds the town and in winter, it keeps us warm.

scenes.narration: On the eve of the feast of the Kings, the fifth of January, the wind turns. It comes from the east dry and sharp. By morning, the water in the bucket by our bed is solid ice. Jeanne's breath is white inside our own house.

scenes.title: The whole country freezes
scenes.narration: In a few days, the whole country freezes. The river stops. The wells freeze. Birds fall from the sky, frozen in the air. And at night, we hear the oak trees in the forest split open with a crack like a musket shot.

scenes.title: Rule one: the fire never dies
scenes.narration: So I make my first rule: the oven never goes out. Not for one night. If it dies, the dough will not rise, the water will not melt and my family freezes. Pierre and I take turns. Every two hours, one of us gets up and feeds the fire.

scenes.narration: Baking in this cold is a fight. Every bucket of water has to be melted over the fire. The dough goes stiff and refuses to rise. So we knead it right beside the oven mouth, and cover it with blankets like a sleeping child.

scenes.narration: At the end of January a miracle. The thaw. The snow melts. The river runs again. People dance in the street. But my father was a farmer, and he taught me one thing: a winter is not over until the wheat is safe.

scenes.title: Hide it or sell it?
scenes.narration: That is when I understand what is really coming. Not just cold. Hunger. Next summer, there will be no harvest. Every sack of flour in this town is now worth gold and everyone knows the baker has flour. So tell me honestly, in the comments: if you were me would you hide it, or sell it?

scenes.narration: The price of wheat doubles. Then it doubles again. A loaf now costs four times what it did at Christmas. Families who always bought white bread now beg for the darkest, cheapest loaf on my shelf. And some cannot buy even that.

scenes.title: Rule three: never close the shutters
scenes.narration: In Paris, hungry crowds break into bakeries. In our town, too, angry faces gather at my door. Jeanne is afraid. But I make my third rule: I sell at a fair price, I sell to everyone, and I never close the shutters. A baker who hides his flour does not survive the spring.

scenes.narration: In March, Margot falls ill. A fever, and a cough that will not stop. Half the children in town are coughing. Jeanne sits beside her all night, next to the warm oven wall. I bake, and bake and pray between every batch.

scenes.title: Dead fields
scenes.narration: In April, the snow is gone. I walk into the fields with an old farmer named Gilles. Where green wheat should be rising there is nothing. Only black, dead earth, as far as the eye can see. He kneels down and cries.
scenes.narration_voiced: In April, the snow is gone. I walk into the fields with an old farmer named Gilles. Where green wheat should be rising... there is nothing. Only black, dead earth, as far as the eye can see. He kneels down... and cries.

scenes.title: Barley
scenes.narration: But Gilles has an idea. 'Barley,' he says. 'It grows fast. Sown now, it can be cut before autumn.' The farmers who can find seed plough the dead fields again and sow barley. Even the parliament in Paris tells them to do it.

scenes.title: The hungry months
scenes.narration: Spring and early summer are the hardest months. There is almost no old grain left, and the new harvest is not ready. People eat nettles, roots, acorns. Pierre and I bake through the night with whatever flour the farmers bring us. Nothing is wasted.

scenes.title: The barley harvest
scenes.narration: Then, in July, the barley comes in. It is not much. But it is enough. The first barley loaf comes out of my oven, dark and rough and the whole street lines up for it. I think it is the most beautiful bread I have ever baked.
scenes.narration_voiced: Then, in July, the barley comes in. It is not much. But it is enough. The first barley loaf comes out of my oven, dark and rough... and the whole street lines up for it. I think it is the most beautiful bread I have ever baked.

scenes.title: The cost
scenes.narration: Not everyone made it. Across France, the cold, the hunger and the sickness that came after took around six hundred thousand lives. In our little town, we buried old people, children and too many of our friends.
scenes.narration_voiced: Not everyone made it. Across France, the cold, the hunger and the sickness that came after took around six hundred thousand lives. In our little town, we buried old people, children... and too many of our friends.

scenes.title: How we survived
scenes.narration: So how did my family survive? We never let the fire die. We stretched every handful of flour. We shared our warmth, and we sold fairly, so the town stood with us instead of against us. And we listened to an old farmer who knew about barley.

scenes.title: Every January
scenes.narration: The next winter is mild. The bakery is still ours. Pierre will be a master baker one day, and Margot still steals the warm crusts. And every January, on the night of the Kings, I keep the oven burning all night. Just in case.

scenes.title: Subscribe
scenes.narration: If you've stayed with me until the last loaf, thank you. Every week, I bring you one more winter that pushed ordinary people to their limit, told by the people who lived through it. If you want the next one, subscribe. And tell me: what would you have saved first?

scenes.title: What comes next
scenes.narration: Far to the east, on the open steppe of Mongolia, winter falls to fifty degrees below zero. There are no walls, no forests, no cellars. Only felt tents, herds of horses and sheep and a family that must keep every animal alive until spring. How do they do it? That story is next. And here the oven is still warm.
